recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this ratio of combinations — what you write each C as, how you split the factorials, and what cancels.
insider_note: The proof turns on splitting (4n)! into even and odd factors: there are 2n even numbers up to 4n, so the power of 2 is 2²ⁿ, not 2ⁿ — and (2n)! must be given the same even–odd split before anything cancels.

steps.label: Write both C values as factorials
steps.margin_note: First mark. ⁿCᵣ = n!/(r!(n − r)!). For ⁴ⁿC₂ₙ both r and n − r are 2n; for ²ⁿCₙ both are n. Then divide.

recall.must_convey: That each combination is written with the factorial formula and the quotient becomes (4n)! times n factorial squared over (2n)! cubed.
accept: write four n C two n as four n factorial over two n factorial squared and two n C n as two n factorial over n factorial squared then divide
use n C r equals n factorial over r factorial n minus r factorial on both and take the ratio
the ratio becomes four n factorial times n factorial squared over two n factorial cubed

express both combinations in factorials and simplify the fraction

steps.why: A statement about odd products can only be reached through factorials, because a factorial is where even and odd factors sit together. Writing both C values out is the only way to start.
common_mistakes: Writing ⁴ⁿC₂ₙ with (2n)! only once in the denominator — it appears twice.
Inverting the ratio and dividing the wrong way round.

steps.label: Split each factorial into even and odd factors
steps.margin_note: Two marks. (4n)! is the product 1·2·3·…·4n. Take the even factors 2·4·…·4n = 2²ⁿ(2n)! out; what remains is the odd product 1·3·5·…·(4n − 1). Do the same for (2n)!.

recall.must_convey: That (4n)! splits into its even factors, which equal 2 to the 2n times (2n)!, and its odd factors 1·3·5 up to 4n minus 1, and (2n)! splits the same way into 2 to the n times n! and the odd product up to 2n minus 1.
accept: four n factorial is the even factors two to the two n times two n factorial times the odd product one three five up to four n minus one
separate the even and odd factors of each factorial, the evens give a power of two times a smaller factorial
two n factorial is two to the n times n factorial times one three five up to two n minus one
factorial ni even odd factors ga split cheyali, even part two power n into n factorial
take out the even numbers as a power of two times a factorial and keep the odd product

steps.why: The right-hand side has only odd products, so the even factors must be taken out and made to cancel. Every even number 2k contributes a 2 and a k, which is why the even factors of (4n)! are exactly 2²ⁿ times (2n)!.
common_mistakes: Writing the even factors of (4n)! as 2ⁿ·(2n)! — there are 2n even numbers up to 4n, so the power is 2²ⁿ.
Ending the odd product of (4n)! at 4n + 1 or 4n − 3 instead of 4n − 1.
Splitting only (4n)! and forgetting that (2n)! must be split too.

steps.label: Cancel and reach R.H.S.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Put the two splits into the fraction from step 1. One (2n)! cancels, then (2n)!² in the denominator is replaced by its split and 2²ⁿ(n!)² cancels top and bottom.

recall.must_convey: That the split forms are substituted, one (2n)! cancels, and 2 to the 2n times n factorial squared cancels against the square of 2 to the n times n factorial, leaving the odd product over the square of the smaller odd product.

steps.why: The even parts were built to cancel: 2²ⁿ against (2ⁿ)² and (n!)² against (n!)². What survives is exactly the odd products the question named, so the identity is not a coincidence of numbers but a fact about how factorials are made.
common_mistakes: Cancelling (2n)! three times instead of once — only one (2n)! in the split of (4n)! is cancelled directly.
Forgetting to square the whole bracket 2ⁿ·n!·(odd product) in the denominator.
Not writing the final line as the right-hand side of the question.
